Alright — **Topic 4** is about something students always get confused with:  
**“Redefining a function in derived class WITHOUT virtual.”**

I’ll teach it in the simplest possible way → with clean theory, diagrams-in-words, and a fully runnable C++ program.

---

# ⭐ **TOPIC 4 — Redefining a Base Function (NOT Polymorphism!)**  
(This matches the CurvedActivity example in your PDF.) fileciteturn0file0

---

# ✅ **1. What does “redefine” mean?**

It means:

- Base class has a function with a certain name.
- Derived class **creates another function with the same name**.
- But since base function is NOT virtual, **C++ chooses based on the variable type**, not the object type.

**This is called STATIC BINDING.  
Not polymorphism.**

---

# 🎯 **2. Why does this happen?**  

Because without `virtual`, C++ thinks:

> “Use the function that belongs to the type of the pointer/reference.”

Example:

```cpp
GradedActivity *p;
p = &curvedObject;
p->setScore(90);   // Calls BASE version! (if not virtual)
```

Even if `curvedObject` is a CurvedActivity.

---

# 🧠 **3. Visual Understanding**

```
GradedActivity
   setScore()     ← BASE VERSION

CurvedActivity
   setScore()     ← YOUR VERSION (redefined)
```

But if the pointer is:

```
GradedActivity *ptr = new CurvedActivity;
```

Then C++ goes:

> “ptr is GradedActivity pointer ⇒ call GradedActivity version.”

Even though the object is CurvedActivity.

---

# ⭐ **4. Why does the CurvedActivity example need redefinition?**

Because your exam PDF shows that CurvedActivity wants to change how the score is set.  
Instead of accepting the raw score, it adds a curve.

Your PDF’s logic:

```
rawScore → add curve → call base.setScore(curved)
```  
fileciteturn0file0

That is the **redefined** version.

---

# 🧩 **5. Simple Runnable Code (Easy Version)**  

Here’s the cleanest version you can understand as a beginner:

```cpp
// topic4_redefining.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

// BASE CLASS
class GradedActivity {
protected:
    double score;

public:
    void setScore(double s) {     // BASE VERSION
        score = s;
    }

    double getScore() const {
        return score;
    }
};

// DERIVED CLASS with REDEFINITION (NOT overriding)
class CurvedActivity : public GradedActivity {
    double percent;   // curve percentage

public:
    CurvedActivity(double p) : percent(p) {}

    // REDEFINED FUNCTION
    void setScore(double raw) {
        double curved = raw + raw * percent;
        GradedActivity::setScore(curved);  // call base version
    }
};

int main() {
    CurvedActivity c(0.10);  // 10% curve
    c.setScore(80);          // → becomes 88

    cout << "Curved score = " << c.getScore();
}
```

---

# 💥 Expected Output
```
Curved score = 88
```

---

# 🎓 **6. Why is this NOT polymorphism?**

Because if you try this:

```cpp
GradedActivity *p = &c;
p->setScore(80);  // Calls BASE VERSION, NOT curved one
```

You will NOT get curved behavior.

Polymorphism happens only when `virtual` is used.  
That's Topic 5.

---

# 🏁 **TOPIC 4 IN ONE SENTENCE**

> **Redefinition = Derived class makes a same-named function, but without virtual, C++ still uses the base function when accessed through a base pointer/reference.**

---

# ⭐ **TOPIC 4 — The EASY WAY (Redefining a Function Without Virtual)**

Forget everything complicated.

Let’s explain it with:

# 🧃 **A JUICE STORY (Super Easy!)**

You have a **Base Shop**:

```
BaseShop
   |
   --> sellJuice()  → gives NORMAL juice
```

Then you have a **Special Shop** that inherits from BaseShop:

```
SpecialShop : BaseShop
   |
   --> sellJuice()  → gives SWEET juice
```

So SpecialShop **redefines** the function.

BUT  
if you talk to the shop like this:

```
BaseShop *shop = new SpecialShop;
shop->sellJuice();
```

C++ says:

> “You are using a BaseShop pointer ⇒  
> I will give you NORMAL juice.”

Even though the shop is SpecialShop!

WHY?  
Because the base function is NOT virtual.

---

# ⭐ **DIAGRAM YOU CAN REMEMBER FOREVER**

```
GradedActivity (BASE)
   |
   --> setScore(s)     // simple version

CurvedActivity (DERIVED)
   |
   --> setScore(raw)   // curved version
```

If you call with:

```
CurvedActivity obj;
obj.setScore();   // uses curved version ✔️
```

If you call with:

```
GradedActivity *p = &obj;
p->setScore();    // uses BASE version ❌
```

Because **variable type = Base**, not virtual → C++ picks BASE function.

---

# ⭐ **WHY IS TOPIC 4 EVEN NEEDED?**

Because CurvedActivity wants to:

1. Take **raw score**
2. Add **curve**
3. Then save final score

Example:
```
raw = 80
curve = 10%
final = 88
```

So it **redefines** setScore.

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

// BASE CLASS
class GradedActivity {
protected:
    double score;

public:
    void setScore(double s) {  // BASE VERSION
        score = s;
    }

    double getScore() const { return score; }
};

// DERIVED CLASS (changes behavior of setScore)
class CurvedActivity : public GradedActivity {
    double percent;

public:
    CurvedActivity(double p) : percent(p) {}

    void setScore(double raw) {  // REDEFINITION
        double curved = raw + raw * percent;
        GradedActivity::setScore(curved);
    }
};

int main() {
    CurvedActivity c(0.10); // +10%
    c.setScore(80);         // becomes 88
    cout << c.getScore();
}
```

**Output**
```
88
```

# ⭐ **SUPER SIMPLE EXPLANATION OF THE CODE**

- Base setScore → puts score as it is  
- Derived setScore → modifies it, then calls base setScore

So:

```
Base: score = raw
Derived: score = raw + curve
```

# ⭐ **EVEN SIMPLER VERSION (BABY LEVEL)**

Base version:

score = raw

Derived version:

```
raw → add curve → then score

# ⭐ **TOPIC 6 — ABSTRACT CLASSES (EASIEST EXPLANATION EVER)**  
(We always learn this before interfaces, polymorphic arrays, etc.)

---

# 🎯 **WHAT IS AN ABSTRACT CLASS? — SUPER SIMPLE**

Think of an abstract class like a class that is **not complete**.

It has a function that says:

> “I have no code for this.  
> Someone else must write the code.”

This blank function is called a **pure virtual function**.

It looks like this:

```cpp
virtual void draw() = 0;
```

The `= 0` means:
- “I have no body.”
- “Derived class MUST write body.”

---

# ⭐ **REAL LIFE EXAMPLE — easiest analogy**

“Vehicle” is abstract because you cannot ride a “general vehicle”.

But car, bike, bus → real.

So:

```
Vehicle (abstract) 
   |
   --> Car (concrete)
   --> Bike (concrete)
```

You cannot create:

```
Vehicle v; ❌ NOT ALLOWED
```

But you can create:

```
Car c; ✔️
Bike b; ✔️
```

---

# ⭐ **ULTRA-SIMPLE CODE (BEGINNER FRIENDLY)**

```cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

// ABSTRACT CLASS
class Shape {
public:
    virtual void draw() = 0;   // PURE VIRTUAL (no body)
};

// DERIVED CLASS
class Circle : public Shape {
public:
    void draw() override {     // must write code
        cout << "Drawing a Circle\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    Circle c;    // OK
    c.draw();    // prints “Drawing a Circle”

    // Shape s;  // ❌ Error: Cannot make object of abstract class
}
```

---

# ⭐ OUTPUT
```
Drawing a Circle
```

---

# 🎯 **THEORY (SO EASY YOU WILL NEVER FORGET IT)**

- If a class has even **one** pure virtual function → the class becomes **abstract**.
- Abstract class **cannot** make objects.
- Derived class **must** override the pure virtual function.
- When you use pointers, abstract classes are very useful:

Example:

```
Shape* p = new Circle;
p->draw();   // Circle's version runs
```

---

# ⭐ **IN ONE SENTENCE**

> **Abstract class = class with missing code that must be completed by derived classes.**

# ⭐ **TOPIC 9 — Polymorphic Arrays (Polymorphic Behavior in Arrays / Pointers)**

This topic is actually VERY easy if you understand one idea:

> **When we use an array of base-class pointers,  
> and functions are virtual,  
> every object behaves like its REAL type.**

This is the whole topic.

Let’s break it down slowly.

---

# 🎯 **WHY DO WE NEED POLYMORPHIC ARRAYS?**

Imagine you want to store different objects:

- Dog  
- Cat  
- Cow  

If you try:

```
Dog arr[3]; ❌
Cat arr[3]; ❌
Cow arr[3]; ❌
```

You cannot mix them.

BUT using **a base pointer array**, you can.

Example:

```
Animal* arr[3];
arr[0] = new Dog();
arr[1] = new Cat();
arr[2] = new Cow();
```

---

# ⭐ **The Magic Only Works Because of virtual**

Without `virtual`, all of them behave as **Animal**.

With `virtual`, each behaves correctly (Dog barks, Cat meows).

---

# ⭐ **ULTRA SIMPLE DIAGRAM**

```
Animal* arr[3]      (array of base pointers)
     ↓
----------------------------------
| Dog* | Cat* | Cow* |
----------------------------------

arr[i]->makeSound();  
```

If makeSound is virtual:

```
Dog → Bark
Cat → Meow
Cow → Moo
```

---

# ⭐ **SUPER SIMPLE CODE (BEGINNER FRIENDLY)**

```cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Animal {
public:
    virtual void sound() {    // VIRTUAL FUNCTION
        cout << "Some sound\n";
    }
};

class Dog : public Animal {
public:
    void sound() override {
        cout << "Bark\n";
    }
};

class Cat : public Animal {
public:
    void sound() override {
        cout << "Meow\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    Animal* arr[3];   // array of base pointers

    arr[0] = new Dog(); 
    arr[1] = new Cat();
    arr[2] = new Dog();

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        arr[i]->sound();    // polymorphic behavior
    }
}
```

---

# ⭐ **OUTPUT**

```
Bark
Meow
Bark
```

Boom — that’s polymorphic behavior.

---

# ⭐ **WHY THIS WORKS**

Because `sound()` is **virtual**.

C++ checks the **actual object type**, not the pointer type.

So:

```
Animal* → Dog object → Dog’s sound() runs
Animal* → Cat object → Cat’s sound() runs
```

---

# ⭐ **WITHOUT virtual (to show the difference)**

If you remove `virtual`:

```
Animal::sound() always runs
```

Output becomes:

```
Some sound
Some sound
Some sound
```

This proves why virtual is required.

---

# ⭐ **IN ONE SENTENCE**

> **Polymorphic arrays let you store different derived objects in one array and call the correct function using virtual.**
